notes: Only 1 run per configuration was executed (runs_per_configuration: 1), so all stddev values are 0 — pass rate variance and time variance cannot be assessed from this data

Eval 2 (L2-有效数据验证) is the sole failing eval in the with_skill configuration, scoring 50% (3/6): the 3 programmatic checks pass but all 3 LLM expectations fail — the agent produced the report file but classified valid records as invalid

The valid-record misclassification ('valid_count: 0, invalid_count: 2') occurs in both the with_skill and without_skill runs, suggesting this is not a skill-instruction gap but a validation logic issue common to both — possibly overly strict SQL injection detection triggering on clean data
Eval 1 (L1-验证规则理解) and Eval 3 (L2-无效数据验证) both pass at 100% in the with_skill run — the skill reliably instills correct rule understanding and correctly identifies invalid records

Without_skill fails all 5 programmatic assertions because validation-report.json is never created; with_skill passes all 5 — the skill provides the critical instruction to write output to that specific filename

Without_skill uses wrong allowed type values ('admin/user/guest' instead of 'user/order/product'), failing the type-domain expectation; with_skill correctly applies the task-specific domain — this is a direct factual knowledge gap the skill fills
SQL injection pattern checking ('需要检查 SQL 注入模式') passes in with_skill but fails in without_skill — the skill explicitly includes this requirement which the agent would not infer unaided
With_skill runs 17.7 seconds faster than without_skill (29.9s vs 47.6s) despite producing a structured output file, suggesting the skill reduces exploratory reasoning and tool call overhead
Token counts are 0 for all runs — token tracking appears not implemented or not captured in this benchmark, making cost comparison impossible

Comparison data shows with_skill (A) at 73% expectation pass rate vs without_skill (B) at 60%, a smaller gap than the direct benchmark delta (80% vs 33%) — the comparison used a different prompt or data set than the main benchmark runs

In the comparison, B (without_skill) scored higher on structure (5.0 vs 4.0) while A won on content correctness (4.7 vs 3.3) — without the skill, the agent produces better-organized output but with factually incorrect content

comparisons.reasoning: Output A correctly applies the expected type domain (user, order, product) and explicitly includes the 'valid_count' field, satisfying two key expectations that Output B fails. Output B uses incorrect allowed type values (admin, user, guest instead of user/order/product) and substitutes 'passed' for 'valid_count', introducing factual inaccuracies despite its richer per-record structure. Content correctness outweighs structural sophistication.

winner_strengths: Skill explicitly enumerated the allowed 'type' values ('user', 'order', 'product'), eliminating any ambiguity — winner reproduced them verbatim and applied them correctly to the invalid record
Skill provided a concrete output schema example with 'valid_count', 'invalid_count', and 'errors' fields, so winner produced a structurally conformant report without guessing field names
Anti-fabrication rules in the skill ('NEVER invent validation errors') constrained the winner to only report what was in the actual data
Step-by-step task structure (Steps 1–4) gave the winner a clear execution path that mapped directly to the three L1/L2 tasks
loser_weaknesses: No skill was provided, forcing the loser to hallucinate the allowed 'type' enum: it produced 'admin', 'user', 'guest' instead of the correct 'user', 'order', 'product' — a factual error that would cause downstream consumers of its output to misunderstand the schema
Without an output format specification, the loser substituted 'passed' for 'valid_count', making its report incompatible with any system expecting the canonical field name
Loser invented extra validation rules not grounded in any schema — specifically a duplicate-id cross-record check and an unknown-fields check — inflating scope beyond what was asked
Loser wrote to 'validation_report.json' (underscore) rather than 'validation-report.json' (hyphen), a filename mismatch that would break any downstream file reader keyed to the correct path

issues: Minor: did not explicitly mention checking for SQL injection patterns in the transcript (Step 3 content check), though this may have been evaluated implicitly
No skill was present to follow — all validation rules were improvised
Invented type domain ('admin', 'user', 'guest') contradicts the correct schema
Invented output field name 'passed' instead of 'valid_count'
Added out-of-scope checks (duplicate ids, unknown fields) not present in any provided specification

improvement_suggestions.suggestion: Provide a skill. The loser operated with no skill at all — every factual error (wrong type values, wrong field name, wrong filename) is a direct consequence of having no authoritative specification to reference. The winning skill's Step 2 alone ('type is one of: user, order, product') would have prevented the most critical failure.
improvement_suggestions.expected_impact: Would eliminate hallucinated type domain and output field name, directly resolving both reasons the comparator cited for the loser losing

improvement_suggestions.suggestion: Include a canonical output example in the skill (as the winner's skill does) with exact field names: 'valid_count', 'invalid_count', 'errors'. The winner's skill showed a JSON block with these field names explicitly; the loser had no such anchor and substituted 'passed'.
improvement_suggestions.expected_impact: Would ensure the output report is structurally compatible with downstream consumers and match the graded expectations

improvement_suggestions.suggestion: Specify the output filename explicitly and literally in the skill instructions (e.g., 'Write output to validation-report.json using a hyphen, not an underscore'). The loser used 'validation_report.json', which indicates the agent defaulted to its own naming convention.
improvement_suggestions.expected_impact: Would prevent filename mismatches that silently break file-path-dependent checks

improvement_suggestions.suggestion: Add an anti-fabrication rule equivalent to the winner's ('NEVER invent validation errors that do not exist in the actual data') that also covers schema invention: 'NEVER define allowed field values or output fields that are not specified in this skill'. This guards against the specific failure mode seen in the loser.
improvement_suggestions.expected_impact: Would prevent the agent from silently substituting invented enums or field names when it cannot locate an authoritative reference

improvement_suggestions.suggestion: Scope the validation checklist explicitly to the five checks defined in the skill (Steps 2–3) and include a note such as 'Do not add checks beyond what is listed here'. The loser added duplicate-id and unknown-field checks that are not in the winner's skill, adding noise to the output.
improvement_suggestions.expected_impact: Would keep output focused and avoid introducing false positives from out-of-scope rules

transcript_insights.winner_execution_pattern: Read available files → Parsed skill's 4-step process → Applied skill's exact type enum and output schema → Produced structurally and factually correct report with correct filename
transcript_insights.loser_execution_pattern: Checked memory and working directory → Found no skill → Improvised validation rules from general knowledge → Hallucinated type enum and output field names → Wrote report to wrong filename with incompatible schema
